questions.stem: A 36-year-old man whose HIV viral load has been undetectable on ART for 3 years asks why he cannot simply stop his medications now that the virus is gone from his blood. Which of the following best explains why ART does not eradicate HIV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-HIV antibodies bind and inactivate the drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: ART kills CD4+ T cells along with the virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free virions in plasma are resistant to all classes

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV mutates too slowly for the drugs to finish the job

choices.label: E
choices.text: Integrated HIV DNA persists in host cells

explanation.summary: ART suppresses replication but cannot eradicate HIV because integrated viral DNA persists in host cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: ART suppresses viral replication, preserves CD4+ T cell function, prevents progression to AIDS, and decreases transmission risk. It does not eradicate HIV because viral DNA integrates into the host genome and persists in host cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-HIV IgG targets virions, not antiretroviral drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ART preserves CD4+ T cell function rather than destroying these cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: His undetectable plasma viral load shows ART is suppressing replication; persistence is due to integrated DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV mutates rapidly, not slowly; rapid mutation is why drugs from multiple classes are combined.

questions.stem: Years into untreated HIV infection, a patient has high titers of anti-HIV IgG and a vigorous HIV-specific CD8+ T cell response, yet the virus continues to replicate. Which viral property most directly allows HIV to evade these adaptive responses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of viral protein expression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Error-prone reverse transcription altering epitopes

choices.label: C
choices.text: gp41-mediated lysis of cytotoxic T lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrase-mediated insertion into B cell genomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protease cleavage of host immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Reverse transcriptase has a high mutation rate, shifting epitopes away from those recognized by antibodies and T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase works with a high error rate. The resulting mutations let the virus evade the adaptive immune response by changing epitopes away from those recognized by antibodies and T cells, so replication continues despite a strong immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: In the chronic phase the virus actively replicates; it is not latent without protein expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp41 mediates fusion of the viral envelope with the host membrane, not killing of CTLs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Integrase inserts viral DNA into infected CD4-bearing cells; B cells are not described as HIV targets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HIV protease cleaves viral polyproteins to mature virions, not host antibodies.

questions.stem: During the chronic phase of HIV infection, the host immune response reaches its peak. Which component of this response directly induces apoptosis of HIV-infected cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-HIV IgE bound to mast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-HIV IgG coating free virions

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV-specific CD8+ T lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophil extracellular traps

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory CD4+ T lymphocytes

explanation.summary: In the chronic phase, HIV-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis of infected cells while anti-HIV IgG neutralizes or opsonizes free virions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The immune response peaks in the chronic phase. Anti-HIV IgG binds free virions and neutralizes or opsonizes them for phagocytosis, while HIV-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis in infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE and mast cells are not part of the described anti-HIV response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgG acts on free virions by neutralization and opsonization, not by inducing apoptosis of infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophil traps are not described as eliminating HIV-infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD4+ T cells are the principal targets of HIV, not the effectors that kill infected cells.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with HIV has serial CD4+ T cell counts drawn at each visit, along with plasma viral load. Which of the following is the principal clinical use of her CD4+ T cell count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confirming HIV infection after a reactive screen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Detecting infection soon after a recent exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distinguishing HIV-1 from HIV-2 infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gauging immune compromise to guide infection prophylaxis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measuring the replicative rate of the virus in plasma

explanation.summary: CD4+ count gauges immune compromise, indicates present opportunistic-infection risk, and guides prophylaxis; viral load measures replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: CD4+ T cell count gauges the extent of immune compromise, indicates present risk for opportunistic infections, and guides prophylaxis such as antibiotics. It is also used to stage HIV (Stage 1, 2, or 3).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A reactive screen is confirmed with an antibody-differentiation immunoassay or NAAT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Early infection is detected with NAAT; CD4 count may remain normal in the acute phase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The antibody-differentiation immunoassay distinguishes HIV-1 from HIV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral load, not CD4 count, measures the replicative rate of the infection.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with untreated HIV presents with painful swallowing. Endoscopy and biopsy confirm herpes simplex virus esophagitis, an infection indicating severe immunodeficiency. His CD4+ T cell count is 260/uL. Which of the following best classifies his HIV infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute phase, because HSV has newly reactivated

choices.label: B
choices.text: AIDS, because an AIDS-defining illness is present

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV Stage 1, because he is only mildly symptomatic

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV Stage 2, because his CD4 count is 200-499/uL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unclassifiable until his CD4 count falls below 200/uL

explanation.summary: AIDS is diagnosed by either a CD4+ count below 200/uL or an AIDS-defining illness, regardless of CD4 count.
explanation.whyCorrect: In people aged 6 years or more, AIDS is diagnosed when either criterion is met: a CD4+ count below 200/uL, or an infection or cancer indicating severe immunodeficiency (an AIDS-defining illness). HSV infection of visceral organs such as the esophagus is an atypical presentation of severe immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The acute phase is the first 0-12 weeks after HIV infection, unrelated to HSV reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stage 1 requires a CD4 count of 500/uL or more, and an AIDS-defining illness is present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The CD4 range alone would suggest Stage 2, but an AIDS-defining illness meets the AIDS definition independently.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A CD4 count under 200/uL is only one of two independent criteria for AIDS.

questions.stem: In the crisis phase of untreated HIV infection, CD4+ T cells are lost rapidly. In addition to apoptosis caused directly by viral replication, which host mechanism destroys still more CD4+ T cells in this phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eosinophil release of cytotoxic major basic protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgE-mediated degranulation of tissue mast cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrophage secretion of anti-CD4 autoantibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophil phagocytosis of uninfected naive T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: NK-cell antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity

explanation.summary: In AIDS, CD4+ T cells die from viral-replication-induced apoptosis plus immune killing by NK-cell ADCC and cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the crisis phase the virus outcompetes the immune response. Viral replication itself causes extensive apoptosis of CD4+ T cells, and the immune response, through NK-cell antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and cytotoxic T cell killing, destroys even more CD4+ T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophil products are not part of the described mechanisms of CD4+ T cell depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgE-mediated mast cell responses are not described as destroying CD4+ T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages do not secrete antibodies; they may serve as viral reservoirs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophil phagocytosis is not a described mechanism of CD4+ T cell loss.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4+ T cell count of 60/uL presents with large, painful, nonhealing perirectal ulcerations. He had recurrent mild genital blisters in his twenties. Which pathogen, reactivated from latency and presenting atypically, is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Malassezia-type yeast

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

explanation.summary: In AIDS, latent HSV can reactivate and present atypically as severe perirectal ulcerations or visceral infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some infections, such as M. tuberculosis and HSV, reactivate from latency when immunity fails. The lack of a normal immune response also yields atypical presentations: HSV infection or reactivation may cause severe perirectal ulcerations or infection of the esophagus, liver, or lung.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV is linked to AIDS-associated B-cell lymphomas, not ulcerative perirectal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV itself does not cause these ulcers; it produces the immunodeficiency that permits HSV reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seborrheic-type dermatitis in AIDS causes red, flaky, greasy lesions, not deep perirectal ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M. tuberculosis also reactivates from latency in AIDS, but perirectal ulcers after prior genital blisters point to HSV.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4+ T cell count of 45/uL develops fever and rapidly enlarging, painless lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows a monoclonal lymphoid neoplasm, and in situ hybridization detects Epstein-Barr virus within the tumor cells. From which cell type does this tumor most likely arise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocyte

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4+ helper T lymphocyte

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dendritic cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue macrophage

explanation.summary: AIDS-associated lymphomas are mainly of B-cell origin, including EBV-driven tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with AIDS are vulnerable to secondary neoplasms. Lymphomas, mainly of B-cell origin, occur at a higher rate in AIDS, including those driven by Epstein-Barr virus infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4+ T cells are depleted by HIV; AIDS-associated lymphomas are mainly B-cell in origin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8+ T cells are not the described origin of AIDS-associated lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dendritic cells carry HIV to lymph nodes but are not the origin of these lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macrophages are HIV reservoirs, not the origin of these lymphomas.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with untreated HIV and a very low CD4+ T cell count has an extensive rash on his face and central chest consisting of red, flaky, greasy plaques. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute retroviral rash

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enfuvirtide site reaction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpetic ulceration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kaposi sarcoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seborrheic dermatitis

explanation.summary: Widespread seborrheic dermatitis with red, flaky, greasy lesions in unusual distributions such as the face and chest is seen in AIDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rashes and other dermatologic conditions occur in HIV and AIDS, such as widespread seborrheic dermatitis, an inflammatory rash with red, flaky, greasy lesions that may appear in unusual distributions such as the face and chest.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The acute retroviral rash is a maculopapular eruption early in infection, not in advanced disease with a very low CD4 count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: He is untreated, and enfuvirtide reactions are localized to subcutaneous injection sites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV causes ulcerations, not greasy scaling plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Kaposi sarcoma is a secondary neoplasm, not a flaky, greasy inflammatory rash.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man in the asymptomatic chronic phase of HIV infection declines ART. He asks how long it usually takes untreated patients to progress to AIDS. Which of the following is the best estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1-2 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 2-4 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 3-6 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 7-10 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 25-30 years

explanation.summary: Without treatment, most patients progress to AIDS after a chronic phase of approximately 7-10 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the absence of treatment, most patients with HIV progress to AIDS after a chronic phase lasting approximately 7-10 years. Adults with AIDS then show fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and generalized lymphadenopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The chronic phase typically lasts much longer than 1-2 years.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two to four weeks is the usual duration of acute retroviral syndrome symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The acute phase spans roughly the first 12 weeks; the chronic phase lasts years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Untreated HIV almost always progresses to AIDS well before 25-30 years.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman with HIV started a regimen containing a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor 2 weeks ago. She now reports vivid nightmares, dizziness, and difficulty concentrating. Which drug is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Efavirenz

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enfuvirtide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lamivudine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ritonavir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zidovudine

explanation.summary: NNRTIs cause rash and hepatotoxicity, and efavirenz specifically is associated with neuropsychiatric effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: NNRTIs bind reverse transcriptase at a non-nucleoside site to inhibit DNA synthesis. Class adverse effects are rash and hepatotoxicity, and efavirenz is associated with neuropsychiatric effects.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enfuvirtide is a fusion inhibitor that causes injection-site reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lamivudine is a cytosine analog NRTI, generally well tolerated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor and CYP450-inhibiting booster, not an NNRTI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zidovudine is an NRTI whose hallmark toxicity is bone marrow suppression.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presents 5 days after condomless sex with a partner who has untreated HIV. He is asymptomatic. His HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay and HIV NAAT are both negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advise transmission precautions and repeat testing later

choices.label: B
choices.text: Begin lifelong combination ART for presumed infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Begin post-exposure prophylaxis today for 28 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Order an antibody-differentiation immunoassay today

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tell him that the negative NAAT excludes HIV infection

explanation.summary: Very recent exposure cannot be detected even by NAAT; advise precautions and repeat testing, and note PEP must start within 72 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: Very recent exposure cannot be detected by NAAT, so negative results days after exposure do not exclude infection. Precautions to limit exposing others and follow-up testing are recommended. At 5 days he is also beyond the 72-hour limit for starting PEP.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ART is for confirmed HIV infection, which has not been established.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PEP should be started no later than 72 hours after exposure; 5 days is too late.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The differentiation assay confirms a reactive screen; his screen is nonreactive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NAAT cannot detect very recent exposure, so a negative result now does not exclude infection.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman without HIV has a male partner with HIV and wants pre-exposure prophylaxis. Her exposure risk is receptive vaginal sex. She prefers a daily oral pill over injections. Which of the following is the most appropriate PrEP regimen for her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily oral dolutegravir/lamivudine combination pill

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily oral tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine pill

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Daily oral zidovudine taken as a single-agent pill

choices.label: E
choices.text: Twice-daily subcutaneous enfuvirtide self-injections

explanation.summary: Tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine PrEP is not recommended for people likely to acquire HIV through receptive vaginal sex; TDF/emtricitabine is appropriate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common PrEP options are daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine, daily oral tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine, or long-acting injectable cabotegravir. TAF/emtricitabine is not recommended for people likely to acquire HIV through receptive vaginal sex, so an oral option for her is TDF/emtricitabine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dolutegravir/lamivudine is a two-drug treatment regimen for selected patients with HIV, not a listed PrEP option.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TAF/emtricitabine is not recommended for people whose risk is receptive vaginal sex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Zidovudine monotherapy is not a listed PrEP option; its role is perinatal prophylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enfuvirtide is not used for PrEP; it is reserved for selected drug-resistant HIV.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man without HIV wants pre-exposure prophylaxis but has repeatedly missed doses of daily oral medications in the past. He asks about a long-acting option. Which of the following is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 28-day PEP course repeated monthly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Injectable cabotegravir every 2 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous zidovudine once a month

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral ritonavir boosting once a week

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subcutaneous enfuvirtide twice daily

explanation.summary: Long-acting injectable cabotegravir, an INSTI, is a PrEP option given every 2 months after initiation.
explanation.whyCorrect: PrEP is antiretroviral medication taken by a person without HIV before possible exposure. Besides daily oral tenofovir-based options, long-acting injectable cabotegravir, an integrase strand transfer inhibitor, is given every 2 months after initiation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PEP is a 28-day course after a specific exposure, not a repeating prevention strategy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Zidovudine's special role is intrapartum and neonatal prophylaxis, not PrEP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ritonavir is a pharmacokinetic booster for other drugs, not a PrEP agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enfuvirtide is not used for PrEP; it is a fusion inhibitor for selected drug-resistant HIV.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with HIV has been virally suppressed on a dolutegravir-based regimen. After she begins taking over-the-counter calcium and iron supplements at the same time as her antiretrovirals, her viral load becomes detectable. Which mechanism most likely explains this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium activates viral protease in host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium blocks CCR5 so the virus uses CXCR4

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron chelates viral gp41 and blocks drug binding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron induces CYP450 metabolism of the NRTIs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polyvalent cations reduce absorption of the INSTI

explanation.summary: INSTI absorption is reduced by polyvalent cations such as calcium, magnesium, and iron.
explanation.whyCorrect: INSTIs are generally well tolerated but can cause headache, insomnia, and weight gain, and their absorption can be reduced by polyvalent cations such as calcium, magnesium, or iron. Lower dolutegravir levels allow viral replication to resume.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protease inhibitors block viral protease; supplements do not activate it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coreceptor usage is a property of the virus and target cell, not something calcium supplements alter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp41 is the target of enfuvirtide, not part of her regimen, and iron does not act on it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP450 interactions are a protease inhibitor/booster issue; the described supplement interaction is reduced INSTI absorption.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with drug-resistant HIV is started on a regimen that includes a protease inhibitor together with low-dose ritonavir. What is the main purpose of the low-dose ritonavir in this regimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds reverse transcriptase at a remote site

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks gp41 to prevent membrane fusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: It blocks integration of viral DNA into the genome

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits CYP450 to raise partner drug levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: It terminates elongation of viral DNA chains

explanation.summary: Ritonavir and cobicistat act as pharmacokinetic boosters because they inhibit CYP450 enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease inhibitors prevent cleavage of viral polyproteins and maturation of infectious virions; they cause GI effects, hyperlipidemia, insulin resistance, and drug interactions. Ritonavir and cobicistat serve as pharmacokinetic boosters because they inhibit CYP450 enzymes, raising levels of co-administered drugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding reverse transcriptase at a non-nucleoside site is the NNRTI mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding gp41 to block fusion is the mechanism of enfuvirtide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking integration is the INSTI mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chain termination of viral DNA is the NRTI mechanism.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with HIV and chronic hepatitis B coinfection stops his antiretroviral regimen, which included lamivudine, because of cost. Three weeks later he develops fatigue, jaundice, and a marked rise in serum aminotransferases. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of anti-HBV activity causing an HBV flare

choices.label: B
choices.text: NRTI mitochondrial toxicity causing lactic acidosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protease inhibitor toxicity causing drug hepatitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid progression to AIDS with CMV hepatitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zidovudine-induced marrow failure with hemolysis

explanation.summary: Lamivudine is active against HBV, so stopping it in HIV/HBV coinfection can precipitate an HBV flare.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lamivudine is a cytosine analog NRTI that inhibits reverse transcriptase and is generally well tolerated. It also has activity against hepatitis B virus, so stopping it in a patient with HIV/HBV coinfection can precipitate an HBV flare, as in this man who developed hepatitis weeks after discontinuation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: NRTI mitochondrial toxicity occurs while taking the drug; his hepatitis began after stopping it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: His regimen is not described as containing a protease inhibitor, and drug toxicity would not start after stopping therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progression to AIDS after stopping ART takes far longer than 3 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zidovudine was not in his regimen, and marrow suppression does not cause hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with extensively drug-resistant HIV is started on enfuvirtide as part of a salvage regimen. Which of the following correctly pairs this drug's mechanism with its most common adverse effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds gp41 to block fusion; bone marrow suppression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binds gp41 to block fusion; injection-site reactions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binds reverse transcriptase; rash and hepatotoxicity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits integrase; headache, insomnia, weight gain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits protease; hyperlipidemia and insulin resistance

explanation.summary: Enfuvirtide (T-20) binds gp41 to block viral-host membrane fusion and commonly causes local injection-site reactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enfuvirtide is the prototype fusion inhibitor: it binds gp41, preventing fusion of the HIV envelope with the host cell membrane. It is not routine first-line ART, PrEP, or PEP but may be used in selected drug-resistant HIV. It is given subcutaneously and commonly causes injection-site pain, erythema, induration, nodules, pruritus, or ecchymosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mechanism is right, but bone marrow suppression is the hallmark of zidovudine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes an NNRTI such as efavirenz.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This pairs the INSTI mechanism with INSTI adverse effects, not enfuvirtide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This describes the protease inhibitor class.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of vulvar pain and itching for 5 days. She also reports a thin vaginal discharge. Her temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Pelvic examination shows grouped, fluid-filled vesicles and several shallow, exquisitely tender ulcers on the labia majora. She has never had similar lesions. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 16

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella zoster virus

explanation.summary: Painful vesicles progressing to multiple shallow, tender genital ulcers are classic genital herpes, most often caused by HSV-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The classic HSV presentation is a vesicular rash that progresses to multiple shallow, tender ulcers. HSV-2 causes the majority of genital herpes, and a primary episode is often more severe than recurrences, with pain, itching, discharge, and systemic symptoms such as fever.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV-1 causes cutaneous warts such as common and plantar warts, not painful genital vesicles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-16 is a high-risk oncogenic type that causes nonproductive, transforming infection, not vesicular ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV-6 causes anogenital warts, which are painless verrucous lesions rather than tender vesicles and ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Varicella zoster virus causes chickenpox; it is not the sexually transmitted cause of painful genital ulcers.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has had four episodes of painful vesicles on the shaft of his penis over the past year. Each episode heals within 2 weeks and recurs at the same location. NAAT of a lesion swab during one episode detected HSV-2. Between episodes, the virus most likely persists in which of the following locations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basal cells of penile epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inguinal lymph node macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trigeminal ganglia

explanation.summary: HSV-2 classically establishes latency in the sacral dorsal root ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV infects sensory neurons and migrates to sensory ganglia, where the genome persists without producing virions. HSV-2 classically becomes latent in the sacral dorsal root ganglia; on reactivation, virions travel distally down the neuron to recreate ulcers at the original site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSV is latent in sensory ganglia; anterior horn cells are motor neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latency in basal epithelial cells is a feature of HPV, not herpes simplex virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV establishes latency in sensory neurons, not in lymphoid macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The trigeminal ganglia are the classic latency site of HSV-1, not HSV-2.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman undergoes cervical biopsy that shows high-grade dysplasia. Molecular testing detects HPV-16 DNA integrated into the host genome of the dysplastic cells. These cells continue to accumulate DNA mutations without undergoing apoptosis. Which of the following viral protein actions most directly accounts for the survival of these damaged cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: E6 binding and inactivating Rb

choices.label: B
choices.text: E6 promoting ubiquitination of p53

choices.label: C
choices.text: E6 stabilizing Rb in its active form

choices.label: D
choices.text: E7 binding and inactivating Rb

choices.label: E
choices.text: E7 promoting ubiquitination of p53

explanation.summary: High-risk HPV E6 binds p53 and promotes its ubiquitination and degradation, so mutated cells escape apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk strains such as HPV-16 and HPV-18 drive production of oncoproteins E6 and E7. E6 binds p53 and promotes its ubiquitination and degradation, allowing mutations to accumulate without apoptosis. E7 separately inactivates Rb, producing uncontrolled proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E6 acts on p53, not Rb.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither oncoprotein activates Rb; E7 inactivates it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E7 inactivation of Rb drives uncontrolled proliferation; loss of apoptosis is due to E6 degrading p53.
whyWrongByChoice.E: E7 targets Rb; it is E6 that promotes ubiquitination and degradation of p53.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a painful cluster of vesicles at the corner of his mouth that appeared 1 day ago. He has never had similar lesions. The physician wants to confirm the diagnosis and determine which viral type is responsible. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Microscopy of lesion scrapings for koilocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nucleic acid amplification of a lesion swab

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type-specific antibody serology of serum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tzanck smear of an unroofed vesicle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral culture of vesicle fluid for 5 days

explanation.summary: NAAT of a lesion swab is the preferred initial test for oral or genital herpes and distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Detection of viral DNA by NAAT in swabs or scrapings from lesions is the preferred initial test. It is highly sensitive, especially early before healing begins, and specific, including the ability to distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Koilocytes are the cytopathic effect of HPV, not herpes simplex virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type-specific serology detects past infection and is used for high-risk asymptomatic people, not to diagnose an active lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Tzanck smear is outdated; its cytopathic findings also occur with varicella zoster virus and it cannot type the virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral culture is rarely used because it is slow, taking about 5 days to grow.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a first episode of genital herpes confirmed by NAAT is prescribed valacyclovir. She asks whether the medication will rid her body of the virus. Which of the following best describes the effect of this treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocks viral entry into sensory nerve endings

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eliminates latent virus from the sacral ganglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prevents all recurrences after a single course

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shortens the outbreak but leaves latent virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silences viral episomes inside infected neurons

explanation.summary: Guanosine analogs such as valacyclovir reduce the severity and duration of HSV episodes but do not eliminate latency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Guanosine analogs inhibit viral DNA replication in actively infected cells, reducing the severity and duration of symptomatic infection. They do not eliminate the latent genome in sensory ganglia, so recurrences at the original site remain possible, and the patient can spread the virus during them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These drugs inhibit viral DNA replication rather than viral entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antivirals do not eliminate latency; HSV persists in the ganglia for life.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Treatment of the initial episode does not prevent recurrences at the original infection site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Guanosine analogs act on viral DNA replication; they do not silence latent episomes.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man comes to the clinic because of several painless, flesh-colored verrucous papules on the shaft of his penis. The lesions are diagnosed on examination, and he is prescribed topical imiquimod cream. Which of the following best describes how this drug eliminates the lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arrests division of infected cells in metaphase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denatures proteins within the wart tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits viral DNA replication as a nucleoside analog

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutralizes virions with antibodies to capsid protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulates immune cells to kill infected cells

explanation.summary: Imiquimod is an immune response modifier that stimulates immune cells to kill HPV-infected cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Topical treatments for genital warts include caustic agents, cytotoxic agents, and immune response modifiers. Immune response modifiers such as imiquimod and interferon alpha act like part of the body's immune cells, stimulating other immune cells to kill virus-infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metaphase arrest is the mechanism of cytotoxic agents such as podofilox and podophyllin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protein denaturation is the mechanism of caustic agents such as trichloroacetic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guanosine analogs such as acyclovir inhibit HSV DNA replication; they are not wart therapies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies to the major capsid protein are induced by HPV vaccination, not by imiquimod.

questions.stem: At a well-child visit, the parent of an 11-year-old girl asks how the routinely recommended vaccine against the pathogen that causes genital warts and cervical cancer is made. Which of the following best describes this vaccine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formalin-inactivated whole virions of HPV-6 and HPV-11

choices.label: B
choices.text: Live attenuated strains of HPV-16 and HPV-18

choices.label: C
choices.text: Messenger RNA encoding viral envelope glycoproteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purified E6 and E7 oncoproteins as toxoid antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recombinant virus-like particles of major capsid protein

explanation.summary: The HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9) is a recombinant vaccine of major capsid protein that assembles into virus-like particles.
explanation.whyCorrect: The HPV vaccine is made from the recombinant major capsid protein of the virus, which self-assembles into virus-like particles. It includes types 6, 11, 16, and 18, reduces HPV infection by up to 90%, and is recommended for all children aged 9-12 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vaccine is not made of inactivated whole virions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The vaccine is a recombinant subunit product, not a live attenuated virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV is a non-enveloped virus, and the vaccine is built from capsid protein, not envelope glycoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vaccine antigen is the major capsid protein, not the E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

questions.stem: Routine cervical cytology from a 32-year-old woman shows squamous epithelial cells with enlarged, dark, wrinkled nuclei surrounded by a zone of clear cytoplasm. Infection with which of the following viruses is most likely responsible for these changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human papillomavirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella zoster virus

explanation.summary: Koilocytes, with large, dark, raisinoid nuclei and a perinuclear halo, are the cytopathic effect of HPV on cervical cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: HPV causes cytopathic effects on cervical epithelial cells called koilocytes. Their nuclei are large, dark, and often wrinkled (raisinoid), and they often have clear cytoplasm around the nucleus (perinuclear halo). These can be seen on a Pap smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSV-1 produces multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions, not koilocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV-2 produces multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions, not koilocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV does not produce koilocytic change in cervical epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Varicella zoster virus produces changes like those of HSV (giant cells, inclusions), not koilocytes.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the clinic because she has noticed several painless, soft, raised growths around her vaginal introitus and perianal skin. Examination shows multiple verrucous lesions, and the diagnosis is made on appearance alone. Which of the following HPV types most commonly cause these lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HPV-1 and HPV-2

choices.label: B
choices.text: HPV-1 and HPV-4

choices.label: C
choices.text: HPV-2 and HPV-4

choices.label: D
choices.text: HPV-6 and HPV-11

choices.label: E
choices.text: HPV-16 and HPV-18

explanation.summary: Anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum) are caused mainly by low-risk HPV-6 and HPV-11.
explanation.whyCorrect: HPV-6 and HPV-11 are low-risk strains that cause anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum), which present as warty lesions in the genital or rectal area and are diagnosed by their appearance on examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HPV-1 and HPV-2 are cutaneous wart types.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV-1 and HPV-4 cause cutaneous warts such as common, plantar, and flat warts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-2 and HPV-4 are cutaneous wart types.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV-16 and HPV-18 are the highest-risk oncogenic types, associated with cervical cancer rather than warts.

questions.stem: A physician unroofs a vesicle on a patient's buttock, stains a scraping of its base, and examines it under a light microscope. The smear shows multinucleated giant cells whose nuclei contain eosinophilic, glassy inclusions with chromatin pushed to the nuclear edge. Which of the following best explains why this test is no longer used for primary diagnosis of herpes simplex infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot show cytopathic change in early lesions

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects HPV koilocytes rather than herpes effects

choices.label: C
choices.text: It detects only antibodies from a past infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires about 5 days of growth before reading

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella zoster virus produces the same changes

explanation.summary: The Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions, but these also occur with varicella zoster virus, so DNA testing has replaced it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Tzanck test visualizes the two HSV cytopathic effects, multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions. Both are also seen in other viral infections such as varicella zoster virus, so the smear cannot establish HSV specifically and has been replaced by modern DNA testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The smear does show cytopathic change; its problem is lack of specificity, not early-lesion blindness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Giant cells with Cowdry A inclusions are herpesvirus effects, not HPV koilocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody detection describes type-specific serology, not a cytologic smear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The 5-day growth period describes viral culture, not a stained smear.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 39 weeks' gestation with known HSV-2 infection comes to the labor and delivery unit in early labor. Pelvic examination shows several active vesicular lesions on the vulva. Which of the following is the most appropriate management to protect the newborn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cesarean delivery instead of vaginal delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Induction of labor for rapid vaginal delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vaginal delivery after maternal serology testing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vaginal delivery after topical trichloroacetic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaginal delivery with a neonatal Tzanck smear

explanation.summary: Pregnant patients with active genital herpes lesions should deliver by C-section to avoid transmitting HSV to the baby.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genital herpes can pass to the neonate during vaginal delivery, causing eye infection and disseminated disease with neurologic, lung, liver, and kidney involvement. It is recommended that patients with active genital lesions have a C-section instead of a vaginal delivery; antivirals before delivery may also decrease transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Speeding vaginal delivery still exposes the newborn to virus in active lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serology detects past infection and does nothing to prevent exposure during delivery through active lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trichloroacetic acid is a caustic wart treatment, not HSV therapy, and should not be applied to mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaginal delivery through active lesions exposes the newborn; an outdated smear does not prevent infection.

questions.stem: A virology laboratory characterizes two DNA viruses isolated from genital lesions. Virus X has a linear double-stranded DNA genome, an envelope, and an icosahedral capsid. Virus Y is non-enveloped and has a circular double-stranded DNA genome. Which of the following statements correctly contrasts the life cycles of these two viruses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: X has animal reservoirs; Y infects only human hosts

choices.label: B
choices.text: X integrates into host DNA; Y persists as a neuronal episome

choices.label: C
choices.text: X is latent in basal epithelial cells; Y in sensory ganglia

choices.label: D
choices.text: X is latent in sensory ganglia; Y in basal epithelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: X is non-cytolytic in epithelium; Y lyses epithelial cells

explanation.summary: Herpesviruses (enveloped, linear dsDNA) become latent in sensory ganglia; papillomaviruses (non-enveloped, circular dsDNA) become latent in basal epithelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Virus X is a herpesvirus (HSV): it is cytolytic in epithelial cells and establishes latency by infecting sensory neurons and migrating to sensory ganglia, where the genome persists as a nuclear episome. Virus Y is a papillomavirus (HPV), which infects basal epithelial cells, where both low- and high-risk strains can become latent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both HSV and HPV are obligate human pathogens with no animal reservoirs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV persists as a neuronal episome; it is high-risk HPV that frequently integrates into host DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the two latency sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV infection of epithelial cells is cytolytic, producing vesicles; high-risk HPV is often nonproductive.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has had tingling followed by small painful blisters on her upper lip every few months for the past 10 years. The lesions always appear at the same spot and heal within about a week. The causative virus most likely resides between episodes in which of the following structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basal cells of lip epithelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sacral dorsal root ganglion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salivary gland acinar cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Superior cervical ganglion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trigeminal ganglion

explanation.summary: HSV-1, the main cause of recurrent oral herpes (cold sores), classically establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-1 causes most oral herpes, recurrent ulcers of the lips, oral mucosa, or face. After primary infection it travels up sensory neurons and classically becomes latent in the trigeminal ganglia, reactivating to send virions back to the original site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Latency in basal epithelial cells is characteristic of HPV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sacral dorsal root ganglia are the classic latency site of HSV-2 (genital herpes).
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV latency is in sensory neurons, not glandular epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV establishes latency in sensory ganglia, and the trigeminal ganglion is the classic HSV-1 site.

questions.stem: A researcher studies sensory ganglion tissue obtained at autopsy from a man with a long history of recurrent genital herpes who had no active lesions at the time of death. No new virions are being produced in the neurons. In which of the following forms does the viral genome most likely exist in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circular episome within the neuronal cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circular episome within the neuronal nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Integrated DNA within satellite glial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrated provirus within host chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linear genome packaged in cytoplasmic capsids

explanation.summary: During HSV latency the viral genome persists as a circular episome in the nucleus of infected sensory neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: Latency is persistence of a virus without production of new virions. HSV-1 and HSV-2 establish latency in sensory ganglia, where the viral genome persists as an episome, a circular piece of DNA, in the nucleus of the infected neurons.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The latent episome is located in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV latency is in sensory neurons themselves, and the genome is not integrated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV does not integrate into host chromosomes during latency; frequent integration is a feature of high-risk HPV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Packaged linear genomes in capsids would reflect virion production, which does not occur during latency.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of cultured cells infected with a virus recovered from a patient's lesion shows icosahedral capsids acquiring their envelope by budding through the inner nuclear membrane rather than the cell surface membrane. Which of the following conditions is this virus most likely to cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Condyloma acuminatum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Flat warts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plantar warts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrent cold sores

explanation.summary: Budding from the inner nuclear membrane is a distinctive feature of herpesviruses such as HSV-1, the cause of most cold sores.
explanation.whyCorrect: Herpesviruses are enveloped, icosahedral, linear dsDNA viruses, and a distinctive feature of the family is that they acquire their envelope by budding from the inner nuclear membrane. Among the options, only recurrent cold sores (oral herpes, mostly HSV-1) is caused by a herpesvirus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cervical cancer is caused by high-risk HPV, a non-enveloped virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Condyloma acuminatum is caused by HPV-6 and HPV-11, which are non-enveloped.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flat warts are caused by cutaneous HPV types, which lack an envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plantar warts are caused by HPV, a non-enveloped virus.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman has a first episode of painful genital ulcers. NAAT of a lesion swab detects HSV-1. She has had one sexual partner, who has had recurrent cold sores since childhood and has never had genital lesions. Which of the following best explains the source of her infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contact with a contaminated surface such as a towel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Latent HSV-2 transmitted from her partner's sacral ganglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reactivation of HPV-6 latent in her genital epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfer of her partner's HSV-1 to her genitals by oral sex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transplacental HSV-1 exposure before her own birth

explanation.summary: Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 cause genital herpes; oral HSV-1 can be transmitted to the genitals through oral sex.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-1 and HSV-2 are spread by skin-to-skin contact via sores, saliva, or genital secretions, and both can cause oral or genital herpes. Oral herpes caused by HSV-1 can lead to genital herpes in a partner, which fits a typed HSV-1 genital infection in a woman whose partner has cold sores.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSV is spread by skin-to-skin contact with sores, saliva, or genital secretions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NAAT typed the virus as HSV-1, and her partner has no history of genital herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-6 causes painless warts, not painful ulcers, and the test detected HSV-1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplacental or perinatal HSV causes neonatal disease, not a first genital episode in adulthood.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old accountant with a long history of genital herpes notes that his outbreaks reliably occur during tax season, when he works long hours under intense pressure. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenaline directly lyses latently infected neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol causes viral integration into host DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endogenous cortisol suppresses immune control

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stress hormones induce viral E6 and E7 expression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stress opens microscopic breaks for new viral entry

explanation.summary: HSV recurrences are most common with immunosuppression, including stress, when endogenous cortisol inhibits the immune system.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactivation of latent HSV can recur throughout life and is most common during immunosuppression, such as periods of high stress, when endogenous cortisol inhibits the immune system. Virions then travel distally through the neuron to produce ulcers at the original site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reactivation involves virion production in neurons, not hormonal lysis of neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latent HSV persists as an episome; it does not integrate into host DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E6 and E7 are oncoproteins of high-risk HPV, not HSV reactivation factors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Entry through microscopic epithelial breaks describes initial HPV infection, not HSV recurrence.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman has just completed treatment for primary genital herpes. She asks when she is most likely to have a recurrence. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Never, once the antiviral course is completed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only after a decade of stable viral latency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only after reinfection from a new sexual partner

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only during pregnancy or after menopause

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within the first year after the initial infection

explanation.summary: HSV is most likely to reactivate in the first year after primary infection, though recurrences can occur throughout life.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 are most likely to reactivate from latent infection in the first year following primary infection, but reactivation can recur throughout life, particularly with immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antivirals do not eliminate latency, so recurrences remain possible.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reactivation is most likely early, in the first year, not after a long delay.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recurrences arise from her own latent virus in sensory ganglia; reinfection is not required.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrences are not restricted to these periods; they can occur throughout life.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with recurrent genital herpes has had no lesions for 3 months. He asks whether he can transmit the infection to a new partner while he has no sores. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Condoms fully prevent spread when no lesions exist

choices.label: B
choices.text: He can shed virus and transmit without symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only HSV-1, not HSV-2, is shed without symptoms

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only uncrusted active ulcers can transmit virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transmission cannot occur without visible lesions

explanation.summary: A person with HSV-1 or HSV-2 can be asymptomatic and still shed and transmit the virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many people with HSV have asymptomatic or subclinical herpes, and someone with HSV-1 or HSV-2 can be asymptomatic and still shed the virus. Condoms lower transmission risk but cannot prevent all skin-to-skin contact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Condoms lower risk but cannot prevent all skin-to-skin contact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asymptomatic shedding occurs with both HSV-1 and HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Virus can be shed even when no lesions are present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Asymptomatic shedding means transmission can occur without visible lesions.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman is evaluated for her first-ever episode of genital herpes. Compared with later recurrences, this primary episode is more likely to include which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single painless verrucous papule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fever, dysuria, and vaginal discharge

choices.label: C
choices.text: No local pain, itching, or tenderness

choices.label: D
choices.text: Painless ulcers that never crust over

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tingling prodrome without any vesicles

explanation.summary: Primary genital herpes is often more severe than recurrences and may include pain, itching, dysuria, discharge, and fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary genital herpes is often more severe than recurrences and may present with pain, itching, dysuria, vaginal or urethral discharge, or systemic symptoms such as fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A painless verrucous papule suggests an HPV wart, not herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary herpes is typically painful and itchy, not symptom-free.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Herpes ulcers are tender, and crusted erosions develop as lesions heal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A primary episode is more severe, with vesicles progressing to ulcers.

questions.stem: A public health team is estimating HSV-2 infection rates in different populations to plan outreach. Which of the following estimates of HSV-2 seroprevalence is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Under 5% among sex workers

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10-15% among people living with HIV

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 40-80% among people living with HIV

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 40-80% of the general adult population

choices.label: E
choices.text: Over 60% of the general population by early adulthood

explanation.summary: HSV-2 seroprevalence is about 10-15% in the general population but 40-80% in people living with HIV and sex workers.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-2 prevalence correlates with sexual activity. Seroprevalence in the general population is estimated at 10-15%, whereas estimates in people living with HIV and sex workers range from 40 to 80%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sex workers have high HSV-2 seroprevalence, estimated at 40-80%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 10-15% is the general-population estimate; people living with HIV have much higher seroprevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The general-population estimate for HSV-2 is 10-15%, not 40-80%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Over 60% infected by early adulthood describes HSV-1, not HSV-2.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is embarrassed about a cold sore on his lip and asks how common this infection is. Approximately what proportion of the population is infected with the usual causative virus by early adulthood?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 5%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10-15%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 25-30%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 40-45%

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 60%

explanation.summary: HSV-1, the main cause of cold sores, infects more than 60% of the population by early adulthood.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-1 causes the majority of oral herpes (cold sores or fever blisters), and the majority of the population, more than 60%, is infected with HSV-1 by early adulthood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSV-1 infection is far more common than this.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 10-15% is the estimated general-population seroprevalence of HSV-2, not HSV-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This underestimates HSV-1 prevalence, which exceeds 60% by early adulthood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This underestimates HSV-1 prevalence, which exceeds 60% by early adulthood.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of fever, drooling, and refusal to eat for 2 days. Examination shows swollen, bleeding gums and multiple painful vesicles and shallow ulcers on the gingiva and oral mucosa. He has never had similar symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 16

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human papillomavirus type 6

explanation.summary: HSV-1 commonly causes gingivostomatitis, especially on primary infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-1 commonly causes gingivostomatitis, especially with primary infection, as well as keratoconjunctivitis and herpetic whitlow. It also causes most oral herpes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV-2 causes most genital herpes; primary gingivostomatitis in a young child is typically HSV-1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-16 is an oncogenic type and does not cause acute vesicular stomatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV-2 causes cutaneous warts, not vesicles and ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV-6 causes painless anogenital warts, not painful vesicular stomatitis.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with AIDS is brought to the emergency department because of fever, confusion, and a seizure. Evaluation confirms HSV-1 encephalitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous acyclovir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral valacyclovir

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recombinant HPV vaccine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical imiquimod

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical penciclovir

explanation.summary: Immunocompromised patients with systemic HSV infection such as encephalitis are treated with intravenous acyclovir.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV can cause serious illness, including HSV-1 encephalitis, especially in people who are immunosuppressed such as those with AIDS. Immunocompromised patients with systemic infection, such as encephalitis, are treated with intravenous acyclovir.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Oral valacyclovir is used for symptomatic mucocutaneous infection, not systemic encephalitis in an immunocompromised patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The HPV vaccine prevents HPV infection and has no role against HSV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imiquimod is an immune response modifier for genital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A topical agent cannot treat systemic HSV encephalitis.

questions.stem: A pathology resident reviews a stained smear from the base of a herpetic vesicle and is asked to identify a Cowdry A inclusion. Which of the following best describes this structure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basophilic granules scattered in the cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clear perinuclear halo around a wrinkled nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eosinophilic cytoplasmic body near the cell membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eosinophilic glassy nuclear body, marginated chromatin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several molded nuclei within one fused cell

explanation.summary: Cowdry A inclusions are eosinophilic, glassy, intranuclear inclusions with chromatin margination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cowdry A inclusions are eosinophilic, glassy, intranuclear inclusions of viral material with chromatin margination, meaning chromatin moves to the edge of the nucleus. They can be seen in multinucleated giant cells or in other infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cowdry A inclusions are intranuclear and eosinophilic, not cytoplasmic basophilic granules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A perinuclear halo around a raisinoid nucleus describes an HPV koilocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cowdry A inclusions lie within the nucleus, not the cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multiple molded nuclei in a fused cell describe a multinucleated giant cell, the other HSV cytopathic effect.

questions.stem: A smear from a genital vesicle in a patient with HSV-2 infection shows large cells containing several nuclei that are molded against one another. Which of the following processes produces these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: E7-driven proliferation of infected keratinocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fusion of macrophages that have engulfed virions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Integration of viral DNA that disrupts mitosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nuclear division of basal cells without cytokinesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Virus-induced fusion of infected cells into syncytia

explanation.summary: Multinucleated giant cells in HSV lesions are syncytia formed by virus-induced cell fusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-1 and HSV-2 induce two major cytopathic effects, Cowdry A inclusions and multinucleated giant cells. The giant cells are syncytia formed by virus-induced fusion of infected cells and may show nuclear molding and margination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E7 is an HPV oncoprotein; it does not produce herpes giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The giant cells are fused infected epithelial cells, not macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV does not integrate into host DNA; the giant cells arise from cell fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These cells result from fusion of infected cells, not failed cytokinesis.

questions.stem: A rural clinic without access to nucleic acid testing sends vesicle fluid from a patient's genital lesion for HSV viral culture. The patient asks why the result will take so long. Which of the following correctly describes this test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amplifies viral DNA at the bedside within an hour

choices.label: B
choices.text: Detects giant cells on a smear in about 10 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grows virus for about 5 days, then antibody stains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Identifies virus by koilocyte morphology in 1 day

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measures serum antibodies to HSV over 2 weeks

explanation.summary: HSV viral culture is rarely used because it is slow, taking about 5 days, with virus detected by antibody staining.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viral cultures are rarely used for HSV. They are more time consuming than NAAT, taking about 5 days to grow, and the virus is detected by staining with antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amplifying viral DNA describes NAAT, not culture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Giant cells on a smear describe the Tzanck test, which requires no growth period.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Koilocytes are HPV cytopathic effects seen on Pap smears, not a culture readout.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Measuring serum antibodies describes type-specific serology, not culture.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man comes to the clinic because of genital lesions that began 12 days ago. Examination shows several crusted, healing erosions on the penis. A swab of the crusted lesions sent for HSV NAAT returns negative, although clinical suspicion for herpes remains high. Which of the following best explains the negative result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NAAT detects antibodies that appear only later

choices.label: B
choices.text: NAAT detects HPV DNA instead of herpes DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: NAAT detects HSV-1 but cannot detect HSV-2

choices.label: D
choices.text: NAAT requires 5 days of viral growth to turn positive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sensitivity is highest in the first days of an outbreak

explanation.summary: NAAT is most sensitive early in lesion formation, before healing begins; testing healing lesions can produce false negatives.
explanation.whyCorrect: NAAT detects viral DNA in swabs or scrapings from lesions and has high sensitivity, particularly in early stages of lesion formation before healing begins. A swab from crusted, healing lesions 12 days in is therefore less likely to detect virus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NAAT detects viral DNA, not antibodies; antibody detection is serology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An HSV NAAT detects herpes DNA; the problem here is timing, not the target.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NAAT detects both types and can distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 5-day growth period describes viral culture, not NAAT.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old member of a swim team develops rough growths on the soles of both feet. He frequently walks barefoot on pool decks and has small abrasions on his feet. Which of the following best describes how the causative virus initiates infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enters sensory nerve endings to reach the ganglia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enters through Langerhans cells of intact mucosa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infects basal stem cells through epithelial breaks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infects dermal fibroblasts through hair follicles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infects superficial keratinocytes of intact skin

explanation.summary: HPV initially infects basal stem cells of the epithelium, gaining access through breaks, even microscopic ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: All HPVs infect epithelial cells, cutaneous or mucosal. Initial infection is of basal stem cells and occurs because of breaks, even microscopic ones, in the epithelium. Plantar warts are caused by cutaneous types such as HPV-1, -2, and -4.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Entry into sensory neurons and ganglia describes herpes simplex virus, not HPV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV infects basal epithelial cells through epithelial breaks, not through intact mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV infects epithelial cells, not dermal fibroblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV targets basal stem cells and requires a break in the epithelium.

questions.stem: Cervical swabs from two women are compared. Patient 1 is infected with HPV-11, and Patient 2 is infected with HPV-18. Which of the following statements best contrasts these two infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are usually cleared by immunity within 1-2 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: HPV-11 establishes latency in the sacral ganglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: HPV-11 integrates into host DNA; HPV-18 is productive

choices.label: D
choices.text: HPV-18 makes abundant virions with marked koilocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: HPV-18 tends to persist nonproductively and integrate

explanation.summary: High-risk HPV (e.g., 18) causes nonproductive, persistent infection that often integrates and transforms cells; low-risk HPV (e.g., 11) is productive and usually cleared.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk strains are often nonproductive and persistent, promote cellular transformation rather than overt cytopathic change, and frequently integrate into host DNA. Low-risk strains such as HPV-11 are more likely to cause productive infection with cytopathic effects like koilocytosis and warts, and are typically cleared within 1-2 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clearance within 1-2 years is typical of low-risk infection; high-risk infection is often persistent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sacral ganglion latency describes HSV-2; HPV latency is in basal epithelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the pattern; integration is typical of high-risk types and productive infection of low-risk types.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Productive infection with prominent cytopathic effect is typical of low-risk types, not HPV-18.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of a rough, painful growth on the sole of her foot that has been present for 2 months. Examination shows a thick, hyperkeratotic lesion on the plantar surface. Which of the following HPV types is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HPV-1

choices.label: B
choices.text: HPV-6

choices.label: C
choices.text: HPV-11

choices.label: D
choices.text: HPV-16

choices.label: E
choices.text: HPV-18

explanation.summary: Cutaneous warts, including plantar warts, are caused by HPV-1, -2, and -4.
explanation.whyCorrect: HPV types have specific tissue tropisms. HPV-1, -2, and -4 cause cutaneous warts, including common warts, plantar warts, and flat warts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV-6 causes anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum).
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-11 causes anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum).
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV-16 is a high-risk oncogenic type associated with cervical and other cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV-18 is a high-risk oncogenic type associated with cervical and other cancers.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is diagnosed with anal cancer. Molecular testing of the tumor detects human papillomavirus DNA. Which of the following HPV types is most likely present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HPV-2

choices.label: B
choices.text: HPV-4

choices.label: C
choices.text: HPV-6

choices.label: D
choices.text: HPV-11

choices.label: E
choices.text: HPV-16

explanation.summary: HPV-16 and HPV-18 are the highest-risk oncogenic types; beyond cervical cancer, HPV is associated with penile, anal, and head and neck cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oncogenic HPV types are capable of causing cancer, and HPV-16 and HPV-18 are the highest-risk subtypes. In addition to virtually all cervical cancer, HPV has been associated with penile, anal, and head and neck cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HPV-2 causes cutaneous warts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HPV-4 causes cutaneous warts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV-6 is a low-risk type that causes anogenital warts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV-11 is a low-risk type that causes anogenital warts.

questions.stem: A physician is choosing among topical therapies for a patient's external genital warts. Which of the following agents acts by arresting the division of infected cells in metaphase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Famciclovir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Imiquimod

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interferon alpha

choices.label: D
choices.text: Podofilox

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trichloroacetic acid

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic agents such as podofilox and podophyllin arrest infected cell division in metaphase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic agents (podofilox, podophyllin) arrest the division of infected cells in metaphase and terminate the warts. They are one of three classes of topical wart therapy, along with caustic agents and immune response modifiers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Famciclovir is a guanosine analog used for HSV, not a wart therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Imiquimod is an immune response modifier that stimulates immune cells to kill infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon alpha is an immune response modifier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trichloroacetic acid is a caustic agent that denatures proteins.

questions.stem: A clinician treats a patient's external anogenital warts in the office with trichloroacetic acid. Which of the following correctly pairs this agent's mechanism with a precaution for its use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capsid neutralization; apply directly to anal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA polymerase inhibition; apply to any surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune stimulation; safe to apply on cervical mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metaphase arrest; preferred for intravaginal warts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protein denaturation; avoid direct mucosal application

explanation.summary: Trichloroacetic acid is a caustic agent that denatures wart proteins; like other topical wart drugs, it should not be applied directly to mucosal surfaces.
explanation.whyCorrect: Caustic agents such as trichloroacetic acid denature proteins, obliterating the warts. None of the topical wart medications (caustic, cytotoxic, or immune response modifiers) should be applied directly to a mucosal surface.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capsid-directed immunity describes the HPV vaccine, and direct mucosal application is to be avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Viral DNA replication inhibition describes guanosine analogs for HSV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune stimulation is the mechanism of imiquimod, and no topical wart drug should be applied directly to mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaphase arrest describes podofilox and podophyllin, and mucosal application is to be avoided.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman who has had multiple sexual partners and a prior chlamydial infection comes for cervical cancer screening. She has never had an abnormal result. Which of the following screening approaches is recommended for her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytology alone, reserving HPV testing for after age 65

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytology plus HPV co-testing to identify higher risk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defer screening until age 45 because she is vaccinated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screen only if genital warts appear on examination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type-specific HSV serology in place of cytology

explanation.summary: Routine cervical cancer screening begins at 21, and HPV co-testing is additionally recommended for females older than 30 who are at high risk for STIs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Routine screening for cervical cancer begins at age 21. Co-testing for HPV is additionally recommended for females older than 30 who are at high risk for STIs, to identify those at increased cancer risk so they can receive more frequent screening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HPV co-testing is recommended for high-risk females older than 30, not deferred until 65.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Screening begins at 21 and is not deferred; the stem also gives no vaccination history.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Warts are caused by low-risk types; screening targets oncogenic HPV and is routine, not triggered by warts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV serology does not screen for cervical cancer, which is caused by HPV.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman who never received the HPV vaccine as a child asks whether she can still be vaccinated. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No; adults receive only topical wart treatments

choices.label: B
choices.text: No; it is given only after an abnormal Pap smear

choices.label: C
choices.text: No; vaccination is limited to children aged 9-12

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes; but only if she has never been sexually active

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yes; unvaccinated people can receive it up to age 45

explanation.summary: HPV vaccination is recommended for all children aged 9-12 years; those not vaccinated as children can be vaccinated up to age 45.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vaccination is recommended for all children aged 9-12 years. For individuals who were not vaccinated as children, it can be given up until 45 years of age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unvaccinated adults up to age 45 can receive the vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The vaccine is preventive and is not reserved for patients with abnormal cytology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ages 9-12 are the routine recommendation, but catch-up vaccination is possible up to age 45.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No such restriction is placed on catch-up vaccination up to age 45.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a sore on the shaft of his penis that appeared 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse with a new partner. Examination shows a firm, round, 1.5-cm ulcer that is not tender, with mild bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following best describes the organism most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enveloped DNA virus that causes grouped painful vesicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram-negative bacillus cultured from a purulent ulcer base

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram-negative rod often seen inside cells on Giemsa stain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obligate intracellular bacterium that targets lymphatic tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tightly coiled spirochete best seen with dark-field microscopy

explanation.summary: A firm, painless chancre with bilateral adenopathy is primary syphilis, caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The primary chancre is a firm, round, 1-2 cm, usually painless ulcer at the site of entry, often with mild to moderate bilateral lymphadenopathy. T. pallidum is a tightly coiled spirochete that is too thin for routine light microscopy and extremely difficult to culture, so it is visualized with dark-field microscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpes simplex virus causes tender ulcers; the lack of pain is what distinguishes a syphilitic chancre from herpetic lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This describes Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), whose ulcers are painful with a purulent exudate and tender suppurative nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis), which causes beefy red painless ulcers without lymphadenopathy, not a firm round chancre.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes the Chlamydia trachomatis subtypes of lymphogranuloma venereum, marked by small papules and inguinal buboes with a groove sign.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a rash and anal discomfort. Two months ago she had a painless vulvar sore that healed without treatment. Examination shows small reddish brown macules on the trunk, palms, and soles that do not itch, patchy scalp hair loss, and several raised, warty, gray-brown lesions on the perianal mucosa. Which of the following best describes the perianal lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beefy red ulcers from an intracellular rod

choices.label: B
choices.text: Condylomata lata of secondary syphilis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gummas arising from granulomatous inflammation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inguinal buboes of lymphogranuloma venereum

choices.label: E
choices.text: New chancres at secondary inoculation sites
