explanation.summary: Raised, warty, gray-brown mucous membrane lesions of the mouth, genitals, or anus in secondary syphilis are condylomata lata.
explanation.whyCorrect: Untreated primary syphilis can progress to secondary syphilis, characterized by a diffuse nonpruritic reddish brown rash that includes the palms and soles, patchy alopecia, and condylomata lata: warty, raised, gray-brown lesions on the mouth, genitals, or anus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beefy red, highly vascular ulcers are the lesions of donovanosis (Klebsiella granulomatis), not raised warty plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gummas are rubbery granulomas of tertiary syphilis that appear 4-10 years after infection, mainly in liver, bone, and testes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Buboes are tender enlarged inguinal or femoral lymph nodes, not mucosal lesions, and are caused by specific C. trachomatis subtypes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A chancre is the firm painless ulcer of primary syphilis at the entry site; secondary-stage mucosal lesions are raised and warty.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is evaluated for frequent falls, especially in dark rooms. He walks on a wide base and slaps his feet down. Examination shows absent vibration and position sense in both legs and diminished light touch; strength is normal. He recalls a painless genital sore about 25 years ago that was never treated. Serum nontreponemal and treponemal tests are reactive. Degeneration of which of the following structures best explains his deficits?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterolateral spinothalamic tracts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lateral corticospinal tracts of the cord

choices.label: D
choices.text: Posterior columns of the spinal cord

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purkinje cells of the cerebellar vermis

explanation.summary: Tabes dorsalis, a form of neurosyphilis, is degeneration of the posterior columns causing loss of proprioception, vibration, and touch.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurosyphilis presents 10-30 years after untreated infection. Tabes dorsalis is degeneration of the posterior (dorsal) columns of the spinal cord, producing loss of proprioception (position sense), vibration, and touch, which leads to a sensory ataxia that worsens without visual input.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anterior horn cell loss causes weakness and atrophy; this patient has normal strength with a purely sensory deficit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The spinothalamic tracts carry pain and temperature; the lost modalities here (vibration, position) travel in the posterior columns.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticospinal tract damage produces upper motor neuron weakness and spasticity, not loss of vibration and position sense.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cerebellar degeneration causes ataxia with preserved proprioception; here the ataxia stems from lost position sense.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for exertional dyspnea. Examination shows an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border. CT angiography shows aneurysmal dilation limited to the ascending aorta; the abdominal aorta is normal. Serum RPR and FTA-ABS are reactive. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his aortic disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gumma eroding directly through the aortic root

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atherosclerotic plaque weakening the infrarenal wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cystic medial degeneration from a fibrillin defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammation of the vasa vasorum of the aortic wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spirochete vegetations destroying the valve cusps

explanation.summary: Cardiovascular syphilis causes ascending aortic aneurysms through inflammation of the vasa vasorum, often with aortic insufficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cardiovascular syphilis, which presents 10-30 years after infection, inflammation of the vasa vasorum (the penetrating arteries that nourish the aortic wall) leads to aneurysms of the ascending aorta. Patients may present with aortic valve insufficiency and a diastolic murmur, as here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gummas are a separate tertiary form, mainly in liver, bone, and testes; syphilitic aortitis results from vasa vasorum inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atherosclerosis typically causes abdominal aortic aneurysms; syphilitic aneurysms characteristically involve the ascending aorta.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cystic medial degeneration from a fibrillin defect is a connective tissue mechanism, not the lesion of cardiovascular syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cardiovascular syphilis is not a valvular vegetation process; the insufficiency results from aortic root dilation.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman who is not pregnant undergoes STI screening after learning that a former partner has syphilis. She has no symptoms, and examination is normal. A rapid plasma reagin test is reactive at a titer of 1:8. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A treponemal assay such as the TPPA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Culture of T. pallidum from her serum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dark-field microscopy of a peripheral blood sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gram stain of an endocervical swab

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the rapid plasma reagin in 6 months

explanation.summary: A reactive nontreponemal screen must be confirmed with a treponemal test before syphilis is diagnosed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL, TRUST) are cheap and sensitive but not very specific, so they are used for screening. Because false positives occur, the diagnosis requires a positive treponemal test (FTA-ABS, MHA-TP, TPPA, TP-EIA, or CIA) as confirmation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: T. pallidum is extremely difficult to culture, which is why diagnosis relies on serologic testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dark-field microscopy visualizes spirochetes from lesion material; she has no lesion, and blood is not the specimen used.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T. pallidum is difficult to observe on Gram stain, so this would not confirm the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting 6 months delays confirmation; a reactive screen should be followed now by a treponemal test.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has a painless penile ulcer, and both nontreponemal and treponemal tests are reactive. He has no neurologic or ocular symptoms and no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G infusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: One intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral azithromycin given as a single dose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral penicillin V taken for several weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine penicillin G

explanation.summary: Primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis are treated with a single IM injection of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin G.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin G is the treatment of choice for every stage of syphilis. For primary syphilis, a single intramuscular injection of 2.4 million units of long-acting benzathine penicillin G maintains sustained low penicillin levels sufficient for cure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G is given intravenously for neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis, which this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Azithromycin is used for chancroid, donovanosis, and lymphogranuloma venereum, not as treatment for syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral penicillin should not be substituted for the recommended regimen because it may not achieve adequate exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three weekly injections are reserved for late latent, gummatous, or cardiovascular syphilis, or latent disease of uncertain duration.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the physician because of blurred vision in both eyes over the past 2 weeks. Visual acuity is decreased bilaterally, and funduscopic examination shows retinal inflammation. Serum RPR and TP-EIA are reactive. She has no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intramuscular benzathine plus oral amoxicillin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G

choices.label: C
choices.text: One intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral doxycycline taken for several weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three weekly intramuscular benzathine penicillin G doses

explanation.summary: Neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis require intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ocular syphilis is a type of neurosyphilis that damages the retina, nerves, and vessels of the eye. Aqueous crystalline penicillin G is a water-soluble IV formulation that achieves the high serum concentrations needed to penetrate sequestered sites such as the CNS and aqueous humor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Combinations of different penicillin preparations should not be substituted for the recommended regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single benzathine dose gives low sustained levels suitable for early syphilis but not adequate penetration into the eye or CNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxycycline is a second-line agent for selected stages in penicillin-allergic, nonpregnant patients; she has no allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three weekly benzathine doses treat late latent, gummatous, and cardiovascular syphilis, not ocular disease.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation has a nonpruritic rash on her palms and soles. Nontreponemal and treponemal tests are reactive. She reports that she developed hives and wheezing after taking amoxicillin as a teenager. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single oral dose of azithromycin now

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ceftriaxone now, without any trial of penicillin first

choices.label: C
choices.text: No therapy until after delivery of the infant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral doxycycline as a second-line regimen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Penicillin desensitization, then penicillin therapy

explanation.summary: Pregnant patients with penicillin allergy should be desensitized and treated with penicillin, the only therapy proven to prevent fetal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin is the only therapy with established effectiveness for preventing placental transmission and treating fetal infection. Pregnant patients with a true penicillin allergy should therefore undergo desensitization and rechallenge under careful observation; a cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone is the typical alternative only if desensitization fails.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is used for chancroid, donovanosis, and lymphogranuloma venereum, not for syphilis in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ceftriaxone is the fallback if desensitization fails; it should not replace an attempt at penicillin in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T. pallidum crosses the placenta at any stage of pregnancy, so delaying treatment risks congenital syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxycycline is an option only for nonpregnant penicillin-allergic patients; pregnant patients should be desensitized instead.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man receives an intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G for secondary syphilis. Six hours later he develops fever, rigors, headache, myalgias, profuse sweating, hypotension, and worsening of his rash. There is no urticaria, wheezing, or angioedema. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An exotoxin secreted by rapidly dividing live spirochetes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of antigen-antibody complexes in vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation to penicillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mass release of PAMPs from spirochetes killed by therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spread of surviving spirochetes into the nervous system

explanation.summary: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction follows syphilis treatment when dying spirochetes release PAMPs that activate pattern-recognition receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within 24 hours of starting treatment, 10-35% of patients develop a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with fever, headache, myalgia, rigors, diaphoresis, hypotension, and worsening rash. It is believed to result from release of antigens and inflammatory substances as large numbers of spirochetes die; these PAMPs, hidden while T. pallidum is alive, activate toll-like and other pattern-recognition receptors en masse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The reaction occurs as spirochetes are being killed by the antibiotic, not from a toxin made by multiplying organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune-complex deposition is not the proposed mechanism; the reaction reflects innate sensing of released spirochetal PAMPs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE-mediated allergy would typically produce urticaria, wheezing, or angioedema, which are absent; fever and worsening rash fit JHR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CNS invasion would not explain an abrupt systemic febrile reaction within hours of the first dose.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought for a school physical. His mother received no prenatal care. Examination shows notched, peg-shaped upper incisors, anterior bowing of both tibiae, a flattened nasal bridge, and linear scars radiating from the corners of his mouth. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this child?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A painless ulcer at a mucosal site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aneurysm of the ascending aorta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent infectious nasal discharge

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raised gray-brown perianal lesions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sensorineural hearing loss

explanation.summary: Late congenital syphilis (>2 years) includes Hutchinson teeth, saber shins, saddle nose, rhagades, interstitial keratitis, and sensorineural hearing loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Untreated congenital syphilis can progress to late congenital syphilis after age 2, with Hutchinson teeth and mulberry molars, saber shins, saddle nose, rhagades (perioral fissures or scars), interstitial keratitis, and sensorineural hearing loss.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A painless ulcer (chancre) marks primary acquired syphilis at the site of inoculation, not congenital infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ascending aortic aneurysm is a manifestation of acquired tertiary cardiovascular syphilis decades after infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Snuffles, a persistent highly infectious nasal discharge, is a feature of early congenital syphilis (<2 years).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Condylomata lata are raised gray-brown mucosal lesions of secondary syphilis, not a feature of late congenital disease.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man returns from several months of work in the Caribbean with two painful genital ulcers. The ulcers have an erythematous base and are covered with a gray-yellow exudate that bleeds when scraped. There is a tender, fluctuant, pus-filled inguinal lymph node on the right. Tests for syphilis and herpes simplex virus are negative. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlamydia trachomatis L-serovars

choices.label: B
choices.text: Haemophilus ducreyi

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Klebsiella granulomatis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treponema pallidum

explanation.summary: Painful genital ulcers with purulent exudate and tender suppurative inguinal nodes, with negative syphilis and HSV tests, indicate chancroid (H. ducreyi).
explanation.whyCorrect: Chancroid is caused by the gram-negative bacillus Haemophilus ducreyi, seen mostly in parts of Africa and the Caribbean. Its ulcers are painful, with an erythematous base and gray or yellow purulent exudate that bleeds when scraped, accompanied by tender suppurative inguinal adenopathy. A probable diagnosis is made when syphilis and HSV tests are negative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphogranuloma venereum causes small self-limiting ulcerating papules with buboes and a groove sign, not painful purulent ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV causes tender ulcers but has been excluded by negative testing, and it does not cause suppurative nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Klebsiella granulomatis causes painless beefy red ulcers without surrounding lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T. pallidum produces a painless chancre, and syphilis testing here is negative.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who recently moved from Papua New Guinea has a slowly enlarging lesion on the penis. Examination shows a painless, highly vascular, beefy red ulcer that bleeds on contact; there is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Syphilis serology is nonreactive, and routine bacterial culture of the ulcer grows no pathogen. Which of the following findings would confirm the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A positive nucleic acid test for H. ducreyi

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chlamydial inclusions in an aspirated lymph node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dark-staining Donovan bodies on tissue biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive nontreponemal and treponemal serology

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spirochetes on dark-field examination of ulcer fluid

explanation.summary: Donovanosis (K. granulomatis) is diagnosed by seeing dark-staining Donovan bodies on biopsy, since the organism is hard to culture.
explanation.whyCorrect: Klebsiella granulomatis, a gram-negative bacillus prevalent in India, New Guinea, the Caribbean, central Australia, and southern Africa, causes painless, slowly progressive, highly vascular beefy red ulcers that bleed easily without lymphadenopathy. It is difficult to culture and often intracellular, so diagnosis requires dark-staining Donovan bodies on biopsy (Wright or Giemsa stain). Azithromycin is the treatment of choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H. ducreyi causes painful purulent ulcers with tender suppurative nodes, unlike this painless beefy red ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphogranuloma venereum causes inguinal buboes; this patient has no lymphadenopathy to aspirate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Syphilis serology is nonreactive here and would not identify K. granulomatis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dark-field microscopy identifies T. pallidum; syphilis serology is already nonreactive and the lesion is not a chancre.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has a firm, painless ulcer on her lower lip that appeared about 3 weeks after she began a relationship with a partner who had a similar sore on his mouth. They have not had oral-genital contact. Which of the following best explains how she acquired this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fecal-oral ingestion of organisms shed in stool

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding to the lip from an unnoticed genital chancre

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhaled respiratory droplets from her partner

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inoculation via microabrasions while kissing an active lesion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactivation of latent virus in the trigeminal ganglion

explanation.summary: T. pallidum enters through any break in epithelium, so kissing or touching an active lesion can transmit syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: T. pallidum is most commonly transmitted by direct contact with an infectious lesion. It gains access to subcutaneous tissue through any epithelial damage, including microscopic abrasions, and inoculation can occur at any epithelial site, so syphilis can be spread by kissing a person with active lesions. The chancre forms at the entry site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fecal-oral transmission is not a route for T. pallidum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The chancre forms at the site of inoculation; a lip chancre implies direct oral contact, not blood-borne seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Syphilis is not spread by respiratory droplets; transmission requires contact with an infectious lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral reactivation describes herpes, whose ulcers are tender; this painless firm ulcer is a syphilitic chancre.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman scheduled for surgery asks whether a blood transfusion could give her syphilis. Although T. pallidum can be transmitted by transfused blood, such transmission is rare. Which of the following best explains why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor screening plus poor survival in stored blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gamma irradiation of blood units kills spirochetes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leukoreduction filters trap the spirochetes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recipients routinely receive prophylactic penicillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The spirochete never enters the bloodstream

explanation.summary: Transfusion-related syphilis is rare because donors are screened and T. pallidum cannot survive blood bank storage beyond 48 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: T. pallidum can be transmitted by transfused blood, but donors are screened for syphilis and the organism cannot survive under blood bank storage conditions for more than 48 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Irradiation is not the protective factor; the organism simply does not survive storage beyond 48 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukoreduction is not the reason given; donor screening and poor survival in storage explain the low risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transfusion recipients do not routinely receive penicillin prophylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T. pallidum does disseminate through the blood and remains in blood during latent syphilis; bloodstream entry is not the barrier.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a reactive RPR and a reactive TPPA on routine screening. He had a nonreactive RPR at a screening visit 8 months ago. He has no symptoms, and examination shows no rash, ulcer, or neurologic abnormality. Which of the following best describes the stage of his infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early latent syphilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Late latent syphilis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary syphilis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary syphilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tertiary syphilis

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic syphilis acquired within the previous 12 months is early latent syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In latent syphilis, T. pallidum is present in the blood but the infection is asymptomatic. It is early latent if the initial infection occurred within the previous 12 months (documented here by a negative test 8 months ago) and late latent if more than 12 months earlier. Early syphilis includes primary, secondary, and early latent disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Late latent requires infection more than 12 months earlier; his negative test 8 months ago places infection within a year.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary syphilis presents with a chancre; he has no ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary syphilis presents with rash, condylomata lata, alopecia, or systemic symptoms; he is asymptomatic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tertiary syphilis (gummatous, cardiovascular, or neurosyphilis) presents years later with clinical findings.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has reactive RPR and FTA-ABS results on an insurance examination. His last syphilis test, 4 years ago, was nonreactive. He has no symptoms, and cardiac, neurologic, and ophthalmologic examinations are normal. He has no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G infusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: One intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral doxycycline given as the first-line agent for latent disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral penicillin V taken for several weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine penicillin G

explanation.summary: Late latent syphilis (and latent disease of uncertain duration) is treated with three weekly IM injections of benzathine penicillin G.
explanation.whyCorrect: His infection occurred more than 12 months ago and is asymptomatic, so it is late latent syphilis. Late latent, tertiary gummatous, and cardiovascular syphilis are treated with three weekly injections of benzathine penicillin G to keep penicillin levels high over a longer period.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G is reserved for neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis; his examinations are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A single benzathine dose is the regimen for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis, not late latent disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is a second-line option for penicillin-allergic, nonpregnant patients; he has no allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral penicillin should not be substituted because it may not achieve the required exposure.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is evaluated for a firm, nodular, nontender enlargement of the left testis. Biopsy shows a rubbery granulomatous lesion with central necrosis and surrounding fibrosis. He was told he had syphilis about 7 years ago but never completed treatment. Which of the following best describes this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chancre

choices.label: B
choices.text: Condyloma latum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gumma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inguinal bubo

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhagade

explanation.summary: Gummatous syphilis, presenting 4-10 years after infection, produces rubbery granulomas (gummas) mainly in liver, bone, and testes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tertiary gummatous syphilis presents 4-10 years after infection with rubbery granulomas called gummas, mostly in the liver, bone, and testes but also in brain and other organs. They may break down into ulcers and eventually cause scarring and fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chancre is the painless ulcer of primary syphilis at the inoculation site, not a granulomatous organ mass years later.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Condylomata lata are raised warty mucosal lesions of secondary syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A bubo is an enlarged inguinal or femoral node of lymphogranuloma venereum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rhagades are perioral fissures or scars of late congenital syphilis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is evaluated for gradually worsening vision and memory. Both pupils are small. They constrict when he focuses on a pen brought close to his face but do not constrict when a bright penlight is shined into either eye. Serum RPR and FTA-ABS are reactive. This pupillary finding is most characteristic of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cardiovascular syphilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early congenital syphilis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gummatous syphilis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurosyphilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary syphilis

explanation.summary: Argyll Robertson pupils (small pupils that accommodate but do not react to light) are a sign of neurosyphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Argyll Robertson pupils are bilateral small pupils that accommodate (constrict when focusing on a near object) but do not react (do not constrict to bright light). They are a possible sign of neurosyphilis, which, along with ocular syphilis, can damage the retina, nerves, and vessels of the eye.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiovascular syphilis causes ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic insufficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Early congenital syphilis presents in infancy with snuffles, rash, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and bone abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gummatous syphilis produces rubbery granulomas in organs such as liver, bone, and testes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secondary syphilis presents with rash, condylomata lata, alopecia, and systemic symptoms, not light-near dissociation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is brought by her daughter because of progressive memory loss, poor judgment, and personality changes over the past year. Gait and sensation are normal. Serum RPR and treponemal tests are reactive, and she recalls an untreated rash on her palms decades ago. Which of the following best describes her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cardiovascular syphilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: General paresis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gummatous syphilis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ocular syphilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tabes dorsalis

explanation.summary: General paresis, a classic form of neurosyphilis, causes progressive dementia and personality changes years to decades after infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Classic neurosyphilis includes tabes dorsalis, general paresis (progressive dementia and personality changes), and chronic sensory and motor deficits, appearing years to decades after untreated infection. Her cognitive and behavioral decline with normal sensation and gait fits general paresis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiovascular syphilis causes ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic insufficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gummatous syphilis causes rubbery granulomas in organs, not a progressive dementia syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ocular syphilis presents with diminished vision or blindness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tabes dorsalis causes loss of proprioception, vibration, and touch from posterior column degeneration; her sensation is normal.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man has had a nonpruritic reddish brown rash on his trunk, palms, and soles for 2 weeks. Over the past 3 days he has developed headache, neck stiffness, and drooping of the right side of his face. He has not yet received any treatment. Serum RPR and TPPA are reactive. Which of the following best explains his neurologic findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gumma compressing the facial nucleus in the pons

choices.label: B
choices.text: A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction to circulating spirochetes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coexisting tertiary disease, since CNS spread needs decades

choices.label: D
choices.text: Posterior column degeneration from tabes dorsalis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treponemal invasion of the CNS during early syphilis

explanation.summary: CNS involvement can occur at any stage of syphilis; in secondary syphilis it may present as aseptic meningitis or cranial nerve palsies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although CNS involvement is typically associated with later stages, primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis can involve the CNS. During the secondary stage it may present as aseptic meningitis (stiff neck, headache), cranial nerve palsies, stroke-like syndromes, or ocular syphilis, as in this patient with a secondary rash.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gummas appear 4-10 years after infection; he has active secondary disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction occurs within 24 hours of starting treatment; he has not been treated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CNS involvement is not restricted to tertiary disease; it can occur at any stage, including secondary syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tabes dorsalis is a late form causing loss of proprioception and vibration, not meningitis with a facial palsy.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has a firm, painless ulcer on the penis consistent with primary syphilis. He declines testing and treatment and says he will wait to see what happens. If he remains untreated, which of the following is the most likely course of the ulcer itself over the coming weeks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes painful and covered with pus

choices.label: B
choices.text: It enlarges into a beefy red ulcer that bleeds

choices.label: C
choices.text: It evolves in place into a rubbery gumma

choices.label: D
choices.text: It heals on its own within about 3-6 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: It persists unchanged until he is treated

explanation.summary: The primary chancre resolves spontaneously after about 3-6 weeks as the immune response develops, even though infection persists.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary syphilis lasts about 3-6 weeks, until the immune response leads to spontaneous resolution of the chancre. Meanwhile organisms have already spread to regional lymph nodes and disseminated, so healing of the ulcer does not mean cure; roughly 25% of untreated cases progress to secondary syphilis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Painful purulent ulcers are typical of chancroid; the syphilitic chancre stays painless and resolves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beefy red, easily bleeding ulcers characterize donovanosis, not an evolving syphilitic chancre.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gummas are tertiary lesions arising years later, mainly in liver, bone, and testes, not at the chancre site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The chancre does not persist; it resolves spontaneously within about 3-6 weeks without treatment.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has reactive nontreponemal and treponemal tests on third-trimester screening; the duration of infection is unknown and she is asymptomatic. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy. A carefully monitored penicillin desensitization is attempted but has to be stopped because she develops a reaction. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment now?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ceftriaxone

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-dose oral penicillin V

choices.label: C
choices.text: No treatment until after delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral doxycycline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single-dose oral azithromycin

explanation.summary: When penicillin desensitization fails in a pregnant patient, the typical alternative is a cephalosporin, ceftriaxone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin is preferred in pregnancy, so penicillin-allergic pregnant patients are first desensitized and rechallenged under observation. If the desensitization process fails, the typical alternative is a cephalosporin, ceftriaxone.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Oral penicillin does not achieve the required exposure and would not be safe after a failed desensitization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Untreated syphilis in pregnancy risks transplacental infection and congenital syphilis; treatment should not be deferred.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxycycline is a second-line option described for nonpregnant penicillin-allergic patients, not pregnant ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Azithromycin is used for chancroid, donovanosis, and lymphogranuloma venereum, not as the alternative for syphilis in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a reactive RPR at a titer of 1:2 on preoperative testing. An FTA-ABS is nonreactive and remains nonreactive when repeated 6 weeks later. She has no genital lesions, no rash, and no new sexual partners. Which of the following best explains her RPR result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asymptomatic neurosyphilis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biological false-positive result

choices.label: C
choices.text: Congenitally acquired syphilis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Late latent syphilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Previously treated remote syphilis

explanation.summary: Nontreponemal tests give false positives in conditions such as SLE (SLAP HIM), so a negative treponemal test rules out syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nontreponemal tests detect antibodies to components of intracellular microsomes, which can arise in systemic lupus erythematosus, leprosy, acute febrile illness, pregnancy, hepatitis, infectious mononucleosis, and malaria (SLAP HIM). False positives occur in up to 5% of tests, which is why diagnosis requires both a nontreponemal and a treponemal test to be positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neurosyphilis would also produce a reactive treponemal test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Congenital syphilis would likewise leave a reactive treponemal test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Any true syphilis, including late latent, would produce a reactive treponemal test; hers is repeatedly nonreactive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: After treated syphilis, treponemal tests remain reactive for life; a nonreactive FTA-ABS argues against prior infection.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man had unprotected intercourse 10 days ago and now has a firm, painless ulcer on the glans penis. A rapid plasma reagin test drawn today is nonreactive. Which of the following is the best test to identify the organism directly from this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dark-field microscopy of ulcer exudate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram stain of the ulcer exudate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light microscopy of a saline wet mount

choices.label: D
choices.text: Routine bacterial culture of the ulcer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wright-Giemsa stain of a tissue biopsy

explanation.summary: Serology can be negative very early in syphilis; T. pallidum is visualized directly from a lesion by dark-field microscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nontreponemal tests turn positive only 1-2 weeks after infection and treponemal antibodies may take weeks, so serology can be negative when the chancre first appears. T. pallidum is too thin for routine light microscopy, difficult to see on Gram stain, and extremely hard to culture, so it is visualized with dark-field microscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: T. pallidum is difficult to observe on Gram stain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T. pallidum is too thin to be seen by routine light microscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T. pallidum is extremely difficult to culture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wright or Giemsa staining of biopsy identifies Donovan bodies of K. granulomatis, not spirochetes in a chancre.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman completed treatment for secondary syphilis 6 months ago. Her rash has resolved, and she returns to confirm that therapy worked. Which of the following laboratory measures is most useful for assessing her response to treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Culture of T. pallidum from blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dark-field microscopy of blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Qualitative FTA-ABS result

choices.label: D
choices.text: Qualitative TPPA result

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quantitative RPR titer

explanation.summary: Quantitative nontreponemal titers (RPR or VDRL) are followed to assess response to therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The quantitative values of nontreponemal antibody titers are used to assess response to therapy; titers can decrease and become nonreactive over time. Treponemal tests are reported only as reactive or nonreactive and stay positive for life, so they cannot track treatment response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T. pallidum is extremely difficult to culture, so culture is not used for follow-up.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dark-field microscopy examines lesion material and is not used to monitor response to therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Treponemal tests like FTA-ABS remain reactive for life regardless of clinical state and are reported qualitatively.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TPPA is a treponemal test that stays reactive after cure and does not measure response.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man was treated with penicillin for secondary syphilis 12 years ago. As part of an evaluation for fatigue, a chemiluminescence immunoassay for treponemal antibodies is reactive and a follow-up RPR is nonreactive. He has had no new sexual partners, and examination shows no rash, ulcer, or neurologic deficits. Which of the following best explains these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active secondary syphilis with reinfection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biological false-positive treponemal result

choices.label: C
choices.text: New primary infection before the RPR turns positive

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistent reactivity from past treated infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treatment failure requiring IV penicillin

explanation.summary: Once reactive, treponemal tests stay positive for life, while nontreponemal titers fall and may become nonreactive after cure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treponemal tests are reported as reactive or nonreactive, and once reactive they remain positive for life regardless of clinical state. Nontreponemal titers decrease and can become nonreactive after successful treatment. A reactive treponemal test with a nonreactive RPR in a previously treated, asymptomatic patient without new exposures reflects past treated infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active secondary syphilis would produce a reactive RPR and clinical findings; he has neither and no new partners.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The treponemal result is explained by his documented prior infection; SLAP HIM false positives concern nontreponemal tests.
whyWrongByChoice.C: He has no new exposures and no ulcer, so a new primary infection is not supported.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A nonreactive RPR and no neurologic signs argue against treatment failure or neurosyphilis.

questions.stem: A clinic is choosing an inexpensive, easy-to-perform assay for initial syphilis screening of all new patients. Which of the following is a nontreponemal test suitable for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FTA-ABS

choices.label: B
choices.text: MHA-TP

choices.label: C
choices.text: TP-EIA

choices.label: D
choices.text: TPPA

choices.label: E
choices.text: VDRL

explanation.summary: Nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL, TRUST) are cheap, sensitive screening tests; treponemal tests confirm.
explanation.whyCorrect: The three nontreponemal tests are rapid plasma reagin (RPR), Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL), and toluidine red unheated serum test (TRUST). They are inexpensive, easy to perform, and relatively sensitive, so they are used for initial screening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FTA-ABS is a treponemal test, used for confirmation after a positive screen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MHA-TP is a treponemal microhemagglutination test used for confirmation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TP-EIA is a treponemal enzyme immunoassay used for confirmation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TPPA is a treponemal particle agglutination assay used for confirmation.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man recently treated for malaria has a reactive VDRL but a nonreactive treponemal test. A student asks what the antibodies detected by the VDRL actually bind. Which of the following is the best answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Components of intracellular microsomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endoflagellar proteins of T. pallidum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specific treponemal surface antigens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Treponemal antigen coated on red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole treponemes fixed on a glass slide

explanation.summary: Nontreponemal tests detect antibodies to a nonhuman lab antigen (components of intracellular microsomes), which explains their false positives.
explanation.whyCorrect: In nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL, TRUST), antibodies produced by patients with syphilis react to components of intracellular microsomes, a nonhuman laboratory antigen rather than a treponemal one. Such antibodies also arise in other conditions, including malaria, which is why false positives occur and treponemal confirmation is required.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies to T. pallidum proteins would be detected by treponemal assays, not by the VDRL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies to specific treponemal antigens are what treponemal tests detect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Red cells coated with treponemal antigen describe the MHA-TP, a treponemal test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fixed treponemes as antigen describes the FTA-ABS, a treponemal test.

questions.stem: A newborn is evaluated shortly after delivery. The mother had positive syphilis serology late in pregnancy and received inadequate treatment. The infant appears well on examination. The mother's RPR titer at delivery is 1:8. Which of the following infant results most strongly suggests congenital syphilis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reactive FTA-ABS result

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reactive TPPA result

choices.label: C
choices.text: An RPR titer of 1:32

choices.label: D
choices.text: An RPR titer of 1:4

choices.label: E
choices.text: An RPR titer of 1:8

explanation.summary: A neonatal nontreponemal titer at least 4-fold higher than the birth parent's strongly suggests congenital infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnosis of congenital syphilis relies on birth parent history, physical examination, and comparison of infant and birth parent nontreponemal titers (RPR or VDRL). A neonatal titer at least 4-fold higher than the birth parent's (here 1:32 vs 1:8) strongly suggests congenital infection. This matters because 60-90% of infected infants are asymptomatic at birth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The comparison that suggests congenital infection uses quantitative nontreponemal titers; a qualitative treponemal result does not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TPPA is a qualitative treponemal test and is not the titer comparison used for congenital diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A titer lower than the birth parent's does not meet the 4-fold-higher threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A titer equal to the birth parent's is not the 4-fold elevation that strongly suggests congenital infection.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old infant is brought in because of a persistent, copious nasal discharge. Examination shows a maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, hepatomegaly with jaundice, and generalized lymphadenopathy. The mother received no prenatal care. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chancroid acquired at birth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donovanosis acquired at birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Early congenital syphilis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Late congenital syphilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neonatal herpes simplex infection

explanation.summary: Snuffles, a palm-sole rash, hepatomegaly, and lymphadenopathy in an infant under 2 years indicate early congenital syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most infected infants are asymptomatic at birth, with symptoms appearing within the first months. Early congenital syphilis (<2 years) features snuffles (persistent, highly infectious nasal discharge), a maculopapular rash on palms and soles, hepatomegaly with or without jaundice, generalized lymphadenopathy, and bone abnormalities. Lack of prenatal screening is the usual cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chancroid causes painful genital ulcers with suppurative nodes; it does not cause this infant syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Donovanosis causes beefy red genital ulcers, not a systemic neonatal illness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late congenital syphilis appears after age 2 with Hutchinson teeth, saber shins, saddle nose, and rhagades.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neonatal herpes does not cause snuffles with a palm-sole maculopapular rash and hepatomegaly.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient asks when during a syphilis infection the risk of passing it to her fetus is greatest. Which of the following maternal conditions carries the highest risk of transplacental transmission?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Syphilis fully treated with penicillin before conception

choices.label: B
choices.text: Untreated cardiovascular syphilis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Untreated gummatous syphilis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Untreated late latent syphilis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Untreated primary or secondary syphilis

explanation.summary: Congenital transmission can occur at any stage of pregnancy, but the risk is highest with untreated primary or secondary syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital syphilis results from transplacental transmission of T. pallidum. Transmission can occur at any stage of pregnancy, but the risk is highest when the birthing parent has untreated primary or secondary syphilis. Up to 40% of such pregnancies end in spontaneous abortion, and all pregnant people should be screened.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adequately treated syphilis before conception does not carry the highest risk; congenital cases stem from inadequate screening or treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiovascular syphilis is a late tertiary form, not the stage with the highest transplacental risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tertiary gummatous disease occurs years after infection and is not the stage of highest transmission risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transmission remains possible in late latent disease, but the risk is highest with untreated primary or secondary syphilis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man who is not pregnant or planning pregnancy with a partner has primary syphilis confirmed by serology. He had anaphylaxis to penicillin several years ago. He has no neurologic or ocular symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory desensitization, then benzathine penicillin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Observation alone, since the chancre will heal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral doxycycline with close serologic follow-up

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral penicillin V with antihistamine premedication

explanation.summary: Nonpregnant penicillin-allergic patients can receive second-line doxycycline or ceftriaxone without desensitization, with careful follow-up.
explanation.whyCorrect: In penicillin-allergic patients who are not pregnant, second-line treatments such as doxycycline or ceftriaxone can be used without penicillin desensitization. Because the evidence base is less robust, these patients need careful clinical and serologic follow-up.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IV aqueous crystalline penicillin is for neurosyphilis or ocular syphilis and is still penicillin, which he cannot take.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desensitization is required for pregnant patients; for nonpregnant patients, second-line agents can be used without it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The chancre heals spontaneously but the infection persists and can progress, so treatment is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oral penicillin is not an acceptable substitute, and giving penicillin after anaphylaxis is unsafe.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with early latent syphilis receives a deep intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G. Which of the following pharmacologic properties of this preparation makes it appropriate for her stage of disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A slow-release depot giving low, sustained levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: A water-soluble formulation given intravenously

choices.label: C
choices.text: High peak serum levels that readily reach the CSF

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid renal clearance within a few hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reliable absorption when taken by mouth

explanation.summary: Benzathine penicillin G is a long-acting IM depot that maintains low but sustained penicillin levels, suited to primary, secondary, and latent syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin G preparations are not interchangeable. Benzathine penicillin G is a long-acting intramuscular depot formulation that releases drug slowly and maintains low but sustained penicillin concentrations, making it useful for primary, secondary, and latent syphilis. High levels for CNS and eye penetration require IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A water-soluble IV formulation describes aqueous crystalline penicillin G.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High peak levels that penetrate the CNS describe IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G, used for neurosyphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Benzathine penicillin's value is its prolonged release, not rapid clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Benzathine penicillin G is given intramuscularly; oral penicillin should not be substituted.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man had a small ulcerating papule on his penis that healed on its own 3 weeks ago. He now has painful swelling in the groin. Examination shows tender, enlarged inguinal and femoral lymph nodes separated by a depression running parallel to the inguinal ligament. Which of the following best describes the causative organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double-stranded DNA virus causing grouped vesicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram-negative bacillus causing purulent painful ulcers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intracellular gram-negative rod forming Donovan bodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specific subtypes of an obligate intracellular bacterium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tightly coiled spirochete that is nearly unculturable

explanation.summary: Lymphogranuloma venereum, caused by specific C. trachomatis subtypes, presents with inguinal buboes and the groove sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Specific subtypes of Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular bacterium, cause lymphogranuloma venereum. It features small, self-limiting ulcerating papules followed by tender inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy (buboes) and depressions parallel to the inguinal ligament (groove sign). Azithromycin is the recommended treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpes simplex virus causes painful vesicles and ulcers, not buboes with a groove sign.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This describes H. ducreyi (chancroid), whose ulcers are painful and purulent rather than small self-limited papules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes K. granulomatis (donovanosis), which causes beefy red ulcers without lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This describes T. pallidum, whose chancre is accompanied by only mild to moderate bilateral lymphadenopathy, not buboes with a groove sign.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman who recently traveled in southern Africa is diagnosed with chancroid after a nucleic acid test of her painful vulvar ulcer detects Haemophilus ducreyi. Syphilis and HSV testing are negative. Which of the following is an appropriate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observation until the ulcers heal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral acyclovir for 7-10 days

explanation.summary: Chancroid is treated with azithromycin or ceftriaxone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chancroid, caused by the gram-negative bacillus H. ducreyi, is confirmed by culture or nucleic acid testing. Azithromycin and ceftriaxone are the preferred drugs for treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Benzathine penicillin G treats syphilis, which testing has excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G is used for neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chancroid should be treated with azithromycin or ceftriaxone rather than observed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acyclovir treats herpes simplex virus, which testing has excluded.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman receives her first injection of benzathine penicillin G for early syphilis. That evening she has a fever of 38.6 C (101.5 F), headache, muscle aches, and chills. There is no urticaria, wheezing, or lip swelling, and her blood pressure is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adding intravenous aqueous penicillin G

choices.label: B
choices.text: Admission for intravenous corticosteroids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epinephrine and permanent penicillin avoidance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reassurance with NSAIDs or antipyretics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switching her regimen to oral doxycycline

explanation.summary: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction usually resolves on its own; symptoms can be eased with NSAIDs or antipyretics.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction occurs within 24 hours of starting treatment, commonly after treatment for early syphilis, and usually resolves without intervention. There is no specific treatment, but symptoms can be alleviated with NSAIDs or antipyretics; it is not a penicillin allergy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escalating penicillin does not address the reaction, which follows spirochete death rather than inadequate therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The reaction is self-limited; no specific treatment such as corticosteroids is indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Without urticaria, wheezing, or angioedema this is not anaphylaxis; the reaction reflects killing of spirochetes, not allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reaction is not a reason to abandon penicillin, which remains the treatment of choice.
